evidence.quote: She was so downcast, so afraid that it should die!
evidence.paraphrase: The mother is deeply distressed and fearful her sick child will die.

evidence.quote:
And the old man
in
 it was Death himself
inhe nodded so strangely, it could just as well signify yes as no.
evidence.paraphrase: Death is personified as an old man visiting the mother.

evidence.quote:
but the old man was gone, and her little child was gone
inhe had taken it with him
evidence.paraphrase: Death departs, having taken the child away.

evidence.quote: there sat a woman in long, black clothes; and she said, "Death has been in thy chamber, and I saw him hasten away with thy little child
evidence.paraphrase: A personified figure called Night appears and reports seeing Death.

evidence.quote: I am Night; I saw thy tears whilst thou sang'st them!
evidence.paraphrase: The woman in black identifies herself as Night, a personified entity.

evidence.quote: "Yes," said the thorn-bush; "but I will not tell thee which way he took, unless thou wilt first warm me up at thy heart.
evidence.paraphrase: A thorn-bush speaks and bargains with the mother.

evidence.quote: the thornbush shot forth fresh green leaves, and there came flowers on it in the cold winter night, the heart of the afflicted mother was so warm
evidence.paraphrase: The thorn-bush miraculously blooms when warmed by the mother's heart.

evidence.quote: Then she lay down to drink up the lake, and that was an impossibility for a human being, but the afflicted mother thought that a miracle might happen nevertheless.
evidence.paraphrase: The mother attempts an impossible act, hoping for a miracle.

evidence.quote: her eyes sunk down in the depths of the waters, and became two precious pearls; but the water bore her up, as if she sat in a swing
evidence.paraphrase: The mother's eyes turn into pearls and the water carries her across.

evidence.quote: every person has his or her life's tree or flower, just as everyone happens to be settled; they look like other plants, but they have pulsations of the heart.
evidence.paraphrase: An explanation that each person's life corresponds to a plant with a beating heart.

evidence.quote:
each of them was a human life, the human frame still lived
inone in China, and another in Greenland
inround about in the world.
evidence.paraphrase: The greenhouse plants each represent living humans across the world.

evidence.quote: the distressed mother bent down over all the smallest plants, and heard within them how the human heart beat; and amongst millions she knew her child's.
evidence.paraphrase: The mother searches among the plants, listening for heartbeats to identify her child.

evidence.quote: I am His gardener, I take all His flowers and trees, and plant them out in the great garden of Paradise, in the unknown land
evidence.paraphrase: Death explains his role as a gardener transplanting human-lives to Paradise.

evidence.quote:
I shall tell thee the names of the two flowers thou wouldst have torn up, and thou wilt see their whole future life
inntheir whole human existence
evidence.paraphrase: Death offers to reveal the entire future lives tied to the flowers.

evidence.quote: it was a happiness to see how the one became a blessing to the world... And she saw the other's life, and it was sorrow and distress, horror, and wretchedness.
evidence.paraphrase: The mother sees two contrasting possible futures, one joyful and one miserable.

evidence.quote: Then the mother screamed with terror, "Which of them was my child? Tell it me! Save the innocent! Save my child from all that misery!
evidence.paraphrase: The mother reacts with terror upon learning one future is her child's fate.

evidence.quote: "Oh, hear me not when I pray against Thy will, which is the best! hear me not! hear me not!"
evidence.paraphrase: The mother relents and prays for God's will to be done.
